title: Phonic launches Phonic-1.1 with more natural turn-taking and a 1.8-point index gain
summary: Want a voice agent that doesn't interrupt, understands pauses, and stays steady in noisy rooms? Phonic today released Phonic-1.1, pushing turn-taking, intelligence, and natural speech another step forward.
ai_summary: Phonic today released Phonic-1.1, a speech-to-speech model, just three weeks after Phonic-1. The company says it ranks first on Artificial Analysis's Speech to Speech Index, up 1.8 points from Phonic-1. Gains focus on turn-taking (DIAL no-turn-taking-problem rate 40.8% to 53.7%), intelligence (τ-Voice 2.0 85.6% to 87.1%), and naturalness (DIAL 4.07 to 4.21). It leads on every benchmark except Cekura turn-taking and Arena Elo. It's aimed at teams building voice customer service, assistants, and voice agents. Pricing and latency aren't disclosed; scores are third-party leaderboard results relayed by the vendor.
brief: Phonic went from Phonic-1 to Phonic-1.1 in three weeks—a fast turnaround.
Turn-taking is the priority: it waits for people to finish, even through mid-sentence pauses, and handles background noise.
Intelligence and naturalness also improve: τ-Voice 2.0 reaches 87.1% and DIAL naturalness hits 4.21.
It's available today through Try now; startup teams can apply for the 144,000-minute Starter Grant.

sections.h: What it is: a second speech-to-speech model, three weeks after Phonic-1

blocks.p: Phonic is a voice AI startup with a team from MIT, Stanford, and CMU. Three weeks ago it released its first speech-to-speech model, Phonic-1; today it follows with Phonic-1.1. These models work directly from speech to speech: you talk, it answers with audio—no separate transcription, text model, and text-to-speech pipeline.

Phonic says Phonic-1.1 ranks first on Artificial Analysis's Speech to Speech Index, run by the third-party AI evaluator Artificial Analysis, up 1.8 points from Phonic-1. It also leads on Sierra's τ-Voice, a benchmark for voice agent tasks, and on David AI's DIAL leaderboard, where human raters score live conversations. Here are the key numbers.

sections.h: Turn-taking: where voice agents most often give themselves away

blocks.p: What makes a voice agent feel off is rarely the wrong answer—it's interrupting or going quiet. Cutting in breaks the speaker's flow; hanging silent too long feels like the call dropped. Phonic-1.1 focuses on when to speak and when to listen: it waits for the speaker to finish, even through mid-thought pauses, and holds up in noisy environments with other voices in the background.

DIAL, from David AI, puts human raters into live multi-turn conversations with models and focuses on turn-taking defects. The no-turn-taking-problem rate is better when higher. Phonic-1.1 scores 53.7%, leading the models shown; Phonic-1 is at 40.8%, Grok Voice 3.0 at 38.2%, and Gemini 3.8 just 14.4%. The higher the number, the fewer interruptions and cut-offs occur.

blocks.p: On another turn-taking metric, Cekura, Phonic-1.1 scores 79, tied with Gemini 3.8 but behind Grok Voice 3.0's 81 and Eleven Realtime v1 Max's 80. So on turn-taking, it leads DIAL but isn't ahead on Cekura. The two benchmarks measure differently, so the conclusions won't always line up.

sections.h: Intelligence: stronger tool calling and instruction following

blocks.p: Many voice agents aren't just for chatting—they need to act while listening: check orders, move meetings, control devices. That requires understanding speech while holding onto enough reasoning and instruction-following ability. Phonic says its models are built for conversations that involve complex tool calling and nuanced instruction following.

τ-Voice is Sierra's benchmark for how well voice agents handle real tasks, run here by Artificial Analysis. Phonic-1.1 scores 87.1% on τ-Voice 2.0, up from Phonic-1's 85.6% and clearly above Gemini 3.8's 65.1% and Grok Voice 3.0's 66.9%; GPT-Live-1 sits at 80.4%.
Big Bench Audio tests audio-related common sense and reasoning. Phonic-1.1 scores 99.5%, close to a perfect score; Phonic-1 was at 98.9%. That's nearly maxed out, so there isn't much headroom left.

sections.h: Naturalness: sounding less like a machine

blocks.p: Naturalness is what makes you want to keep talking. It covers pacing, emotional inflections, and conversationalness. DIAL's human raters gave Phonic-1.1 a naturalness score of 4.21, leading the models shown. Phonic-1 scored 4.07, GPT-Live-1 3.91, Grok Voice 3.0 3.57, and Gemini 3.8 2.81.
Note: the 4.21 isn't on the same scale as the 53.7% or 87.1% above, so don't compare those numbers directly. It only compares within the naturalness row.
Looking at the three improvement areas in this release, turn-taking is the one Phonic emphasizes most.

sections.h: All seven benchmarks: who leads where?

blocks.p: The full picture is in one table: seven benchmarks across the models. Each row only works horizontally—percentages, Elo scores, and a 4-point naturalness scale all use different units.

fig.title: Complete scores across the seven benchmarks, compared row by row
fig.subtitle: Compare only within each row; units differ (%, Elo, 4-point scale)
fig.note: Gemini 3.8 = Gemini 3.8 Live (Extended Thinking, high); Grok 3.0 = Grok Voice 3.0; GPT-Live-1 = Astra, medium; Eleven Max = Eleven Realtime v1 Max

blocks.p: From the table: Phonic-1.1 leads every benchmark except Cekura turn-taking and Arena Elo. Those go to Grok Voice 3.0 at 81 points and 1059 Elo. Arena Elo is an arena score where humans listen blind and pick winners; Phonic-1.1 sits second at 1046. So leading the index doesn't mean winning every row.

sections.h: How to use it, and what it costs

blocks.p: Phonic-1.1 is available starting today: the site has Try now and Docs. The announcement doesn't list a per-million-token or per-minute price; check Docs or contact Phonic.

callout.title: Starter Grant for startups
callout.text: If you're a startup building voice products, you can apply for the Speech-to-Speech Starter Grant: 144,000 minutes of Phonic usage over 12 months, plus a dedicated Slack channel with direct access to Phonic's research and engineering team.

list: Pricing: no per-minute or per-million-token price is listed.
Latency: no figure for how long from when the user stops speaking to when the AI responds.
Supported languages and accent coverage: not stated.
Model size, training data, and the specific changes: not stated.
Standard plans beyond the Starter Grant, including concurrency limits: not stated.
Which other models and configurations appear on the full leaderboard: only these rivals are listed; see Artificial Analysis for the full ranking.

blocks.p: The value is clear: it waits better, thinks better, and sounds more natural. Teams building voice customer service, voice assistants, or in-meeting voice agents should benefit directly—especially in scenarios that need complex tool calling and are prone to interruption problems.

The tradeoffs and caveats: pricing is unknown; Cekura turn-taking and Arena Elo still trail Grok Voice 3.0; and all scores above come from third-party leaderboards as relayed by Phonic's blog, so verify them in the leaderboards and your own trials before choosing.

list: If you're building voice agents that call tools, or interruptions are a real pain: it's worth applying for a trial and the Starter Grant.
If you care most about overall chat preference (Arena Elo): Grok Voice 3.0 still leads there, so compare it side by side.
If you only care about price: no numbers are given here—check Docs or contact Phonic separately.
